1:
The title names Moses, and the entry divides over whether it can be believed. Adam Clarke reports that all the versions ascribe the psalm to him and that one specifies the occasion, a prayer made when the people had sinned in the wilderness; but it cannot be the lawgiver’s, since the age of man was not then seventy or eighty as the psalm states — Joshua lived a hundred and ten years, Moses himself a hundred and twenty, his brother a hundred and twenty-three, and their contemporaries in the same proportion — so that if the title is authentic it must refer to some other person. Keil and Delitzsch defend it as strongly as any inscription in the psalter: there is scarcely any written memorial of antiquity which so brilliantly justifies the testimony of tradition concerning its origin, and the psalm comes out of the midst of the dying off of the older generation during the march through the wilderness; they suggest it was preserved in one of the older books, as Matthew Henry also guesses. Augustine of Hippo calls Moses the minister of the old covenant and the prophet of the new. John Calvin takes it for Moses consoling a people subject to the common law of mortality.

On the dwelling place Charles Ellicott notes that the Greek and Latin read refuge, probably from a different word, but keeps the sense of a continued abode, which he says strikes the psalm’s key-note: the short duration of each succeeding generation is contrasted with the eternity of God, so that even the transient creatures of an hour may come to feel secure and at home. C.H. Spurgeon reads it from the desert: wanderers though they be in a howling wilderness, they find a home in God, as their forefathers did who dwelt in tents among the Canaanites; foxes have holes and birds nests, but the saints dwell in their God. John Gill makes the same point historically, that the patriarchs dwelt in a strange land and their posterity in a land not theirs, and yet God was the habitation of all who trusted him. On the eternity Adam Clarke gives the Latin formula, from the eternity that is past before time began to the eternity that is after, when time shall have an end, and calls it the highest description of God’s eternity human language can reach. Charles Ellicott prefers a progressive parallelism, before the mountains were born or ever the earth and world brought forth, that is before vegetation or life appeared.

The third verse is read as sentence or as promise. John Wesley hears the sad sentence that man return to the dust out of which he was taken. Adam Clarke hears the opposite, a clear and strong promise of the resurrection of the body after it has long slept mingled with the dust. Charles Ellicott makes it neither, but the succession of generations, one dying and another bidden turn and succeed it. The verse that follows divides the entry more sharply still. John Gill uses it against an objection to the resurrection drawn from the time some have lain in the grave: since a thousand years are but one day with God, a man lying six or seven thousand years would be there but so many days. Adam Clarke puts the same argument and adds that the author probably has also in view the shortening of human life from a thousand years to threescore and ten. Charles Ellicott refuses the arithmetic altogether: the verse had already begun to receive such treatment, and to be made the basis of millenarian computations, when the second apostolic epistle was written, whereas it merely contrasts divine unchangeableness with the vicissitudes of a brief life. He sets beside it two poets, one on all our yesterdays lighting fools the way to dusty death, and one verse rendering of this psalm.
5:
Adam Clarke sets out the imagery of these verses as a system. Life is a stream ever gliding away, sometimes a mighty torrent when plague or famine or war sweeps away thousands daily, and sometimes a rapid one when the young are suddenly carried off by fever; youth is the morning, the decline of life the evening, death a sleep, and the resurrection the return of the flowers in spring — and the whole of life is like a sleep or a dream, since the eternal world is the real one and all here is shadowy or representative. John Wesley keeps to the sweep of it, that mankind is carried away universally, without exception or distinction, and that a sleep is short and vain and not minded till it is past. John Gill hears an allusion to the deluge in the flood, and reads the flourishing grass of the young man growing in stature and in the endowments of his mind, and perhaps in riches, adding that it is well if he grows in grace too.

Whether the consumption is universal or national divides the entry. Charles Ellicott puts the weight on the change of person: the plural shows that the poet was not merely moralising on the brevity of human life but uttering a dirge over the departed glory of Israel, since instead of proving superior to vicissitude the covenant race had shared it. Matthew Henry reads it the same way, that Moses teaches the people to confess the sentence they were under in a special manner, their share in the common lot of mortality not being enough. John Gill makes them the Israelites in the wilderness owning that they were wasting there as it had been threatened, and notes that one Jewish commentator applies the words to the captivity instead. Adam Clarke takes the verse universally: death would not have entered the world if men had not fallen from God, and pain, disease and sickness are so many proofs of our defection from original rectitude, so that even in a protracted life we consume away and only seem to live in order to die; he adds a verse about wasting lives growing shorter as the months increase.

The last verse of the section turns on an unusual word. Charles Ellicott observes that the phrase about the light of God’s countenance usually means favour, but that the word here rendered light is not the one used in that expression and means rather a body of light, so that the sense is the sun, or the eye, of God’s countenance; he sets beside it a line in which a god opens his eye of anger upon the accursed. He would also keep the singular of the original and render it our secret character rather than our secret sins. Adam Clarke reaches the same picture from the other side: sins committed in darkness and privacy are easily discovered, being shown by the splendours of the divine face shining upon them, as we light a candle and carry it into a dark place to discover what is there. John Wesley takes the secret sins for those hidden from the eyes of men but brought to light by God’s judgments. John Gill makes the setting of sins before God the evidence on which a righteous judge proceeds, and notes that it is the exact opposite of pardon, which is described as casting them behind his back.
9:
What our years are spent as divides the entry before anything else. Adam Clarke reports that the Latin has them passing away like the years of the spider, and that all the versions have the word though it appears neither in the Hebrew nor in any manuscript yet collated; he gives his old Psalter’s paraphrase of it — that as the spider makes vain webs to take flies with guile, so our years are occupied in idle and deceitful casts about earthly things and pass without fruit of good works — but the Hebrew, he says, differs from all the versions and means that we consume our years like a groan: we live a dying, whining, complaining life, and at last a groan is its termination. Charles Ellicott reaches nearly the same word, rendering it a murmur and, from the parallelism with wrath, a moan of sadness; he notes that since the cognate verb often means to meditate some render it thought, and quotes the line that gallant youth speeds by like a thought.

Adam Clarke returns at the tenth verse to his argument against the title, since the term of human life was much longer when Moses flourished than eighty years at the most, many living a hundred years even in David’s time; and he takes the strength that is labour and sorrow for the infirmities of old age, the body being cut off while the immortal spirit wings its way into the eternal world. John Gill takes the same figures as history rather than objection, tracing the shortening of life from nine hundred years before the flood to a hundred and twenty after it and to seventy in the time of Moses, and observing that of those numbered in the wilderness none were left but two. Charles Ellicott finds the received clause about being soon cut off unable to give the reason it professes to give, and would render instead that there comes a haste that we may fly away: even though we may have prayed for an extension of life, it brings with it such weariness that we long at last to escape — and he sets beside it a poet’s lines on feet swift-winged with desire to get a grave.

On the question who knows the power of the anger Charles Ellicott would render it who regardeth thy anger, and adds that only those have that just terror who possess the bowed apprehension called the fear of God — while those who scoff at religion often become the victims of a wild and base terror. John Gill instances the drowning of the old world and the consumption in the wilderness, and observes that those in hell know that anger experimentally while men on earth rarely attend to it. The petition that follows is where Charles Ellicott stands alone. The verse literally gives, in allotting our days so teach; and the natural way to take it is to make God, not man, the reckoner — in allotting our days thus make us know, that we may present a wise heart. The ordinary rendering, he grants, has given birth to a number of sayings, but it is neither very intelligible in itself nor supportable from the original except by one late instance. John Gill builds on the received words and distinguishes: it is not counting arithmetically, for which no divine teaching is needed, nor calculating the time to come, which no man can do, but numbering the days as if the present were the last. C.H. Spurgeon puts it that numeration is a child’s exercise in arithmetic, yet to number their days aright the best of men need the Lord’s teaching, since we are more anxious to count the stars than our days. Matthew Henry calls it an excellent art, and John Wesley makes it a consideration of the certainty and speediness of death.
13:
Charles Ellicott would render the opening petition turn rather than return, and takes the close of the psalm as the experience of some particular epoch and a prayer for Israel: from his meditation on the shortness of human existence the poet does not pass to a prayer for a prolonged life of his own, like Hezekiah, but for some intervention in relief of the suffering community of which he forms part; and where the received text asks God to repent, he would read have pity. John Gill allows two senses of the return — from the fierceness of anger, on the authority of Aben Ezra and Jarchi, or to the people from whom God had departed — and guards the second: though God is everywhere as to his being and immensity, his gracious presence is not, and he sometimes withdraws it. Adam Clarke takes the repenting as being comforted, rejoicing over them to do them good, and asks that God be glorified rather in their salvation than in their destruction. John Wesley reads it simply as a return to us in mercy.

What the morning means divides them mildly. John Gill reports that the word may be rendered in the morning, which some understand literally of the beginning of the day and so a foundation for joy the whole day following, some of the morning of the resurrection, and others, with Kimchi and Jarchi, of the day of redemption; he applies it himself to the morning of the gospel dispensation and to Christ, the mercy promised to the fathers, whose coming was prepared as the morning. Charles Ellicott keeps it inside the situation of the psalm: the morning of new hope and courage after the night of affliction is spent. Adam Clarke asks that mercy shine now, so that it shall seem the morning of their days. John Wesley gives one word for it: speedily. On the gladness measured against the affliction John Gill thinks no exact number is meant but a proportion, a believer’s life being a chequer of black and white; and he adds that between the joy of heaven and present affliction there is no proportion at all.

Adam Clarke reads the same request historically — as many years of prosperity as of adversity, since they have now suffered seventy years of a most distressful captivity — and carries that dating to the end, taking the establishing of the work of their hands as the rebuilding of the temple which the surrounding heathens and Samaritans wished to hinder, and asking that the top-stone be brought on with shouting; he adds that the closing repetition is wanting in three of Kennicott’s manuscripts, in the Targum, the Septuagint and the Ethiopic, and that if genuine it marks great earnestness. Charles Ellicott keeps only the proportion: a prayer that prosperity may follow what has been endured. Where the work is to appear, John Gill offers three readings and settles on none — the providence that conducted the people through the wilderness into Canaan, the work of redemption by the Messiah, then promised but not yet shown, or the work of grace upon the heart, which is internal and not obvious to view and must be shone upon before it is manifest. On the beauty of the Lord Charles Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word, like the Greek term and like our own grace, seems to combine beauty and favour. John Gill runs through that range too — the gracious presence that makes his tabernacles amiable, the righteousness of Christ put on his people as comeliness, the beauty of holiness — and then presses past it: the words may be rendered let the beauty of the Lord be with us, and the beauty may be Christ himself, white and ruddy, appearing as the Immanuel. John Wesley asks that God not only work for them but in them.
